Pokkep's Attempt To Produce Actual Content (PATPAC) - 1: An Introduction to Buddhism, Part I:

Opening Statements:

  • Buddhism is fundamentally not a religion, a belief system or system of doctrines. It can be most effectively defined as a conversation. Buddhism cannot be explicitly taught but can be discussed and practised. You don't 'join' Buddhism, you just start doing it, exactly how to practise will come in later.

  • The word 'Buddha' is a title which can be interpreted in many different ways. The most common interpretation is 'Enlightened One', but a more practical and down-to-earth interpretation is 'Someone Who Has Woken Up'. The historical Buddha was named Siddartha Gautama and he was quite simply a man in his mid-thirties who liked to think about reality. He is not to be worshipped or praised, Siddartha was simply a teacher of his own philosophy.

  • There was not and there cannot be just one Buddha. Everyone can attain Buddhahood and it isn't something that you can really assign to yourself. If you wake up one day and say 'Hey I'm a Buddha because I'm ever so enlightened and awake!' then you are are not a Buddha, you're probably a little bit arrogant and are yet to be enlightened further.

  • In essence, Buddhism is the discipline of minimizing and eventually eliminating suffering by eliminating cravings, desires and ignorance.

  • Buddhism (and it's philosophical friend Taoism of which I know nothing) has been a huge inspiration in the development of many schools of thought and religious doctrines. Jesus' teachings were mostly Buddhist philosophy through the lens of Judaism. Because of this, Buddhism has become distorted over the years to the point where you can pass anything off as Buddhist if you try. See Zizek's criticism of Buddhism for a fascinating (or should I say faschkinatshing) deconstruction of this.

  • Because of this, Buddhist philosophy or discourse and the way it is interpreted can vary from person to person. No two books, documents or conversations on Buddhism will ever fully agree. Thus, even right now, what I am writing is my interpretation of the Buddhism that I have practised.

  • This is an introduction, not a definitive paper and I will aim to release a new part consistently depending on the reception of this part, if you have a point to argue - please - argue it. The whole point of this is to discuss and eliminate ignorance. If I've said something contradictory, hurtful or outright wrong then please - correct me. Such is the discipline of Buddhism.

Tathatā:

I am starting off this discourse a bit weirdly by first discussing Tathatā. In my opinion, although this idea was formally developed later than Siddartha's original teachings, it is central in understanding his thought process and the development of Buddhist dielectic. The concept of tathatā is absolutely fundamental to the discourse of Buddhist philosophy and as such is one of the few times I will actually use the non-westernised word for a concept. Tathatā is experience incarnate. It's the feeling you get when you see someone's face light up when they smile. It's the feeling you get when you step into the cold night, look up and feel truly awed by the sheer expanse above. It's feeling the wind in your hair or the smoothness of a pebble on the beach. It is the experience of experience in it's totality. To put it simply Tathatā is the realisation that miracles are not acts which subvert nature but that nature is in fact a miracle. It is often compared to the early sound a child experiencing wonder makes Ta Ta Ta/Da Da Da/Ma Ma Ma.

  • Tathatā means 'suchness' or 'thusness' and is composed of ten 'suchnesses' at any given moment. The (arguably and for the sake of concise posting) four most important suchnesses go as follows:

  • Such a Form (1): Everything that is discernible about a moment/event/object. Colour, taste, sound, temperature, weight, etc. This one is pretty self-explanatory, 'This rock I am holding is smooth, black, heavy and hard'. Simple.

  • Such a Nature (2): Everything that is not discernible about a moment/event/object. This is essence of an experience or an appreciation of the inherent quality of whatever you're experiencing. For example, a rollercoaster ride is thrilling not just because of the g-force felt by the rider, g-force is also felt when on an aeroplane or a fast lift and these experiences are clearly different. Exactly what this is is a little tough to pin down but keep at it, we all understand eventually.

  • Such an Entity (3): Everything that is experienced about a moment/event/object whether discernible or not. This is the feeling you get when you see a loved one, you don't know why you feel the way you do, it's not just because of the way they talk or walk or smell or feel, it's because of the way they are.

  • Here I'm going to take a short interlude to summarise the penultimate six of the ten suchnesses. Quite simply, the last three describe the reality of experience, the next six(4-9) describe the purpose and workings of experience. For example, it is the purpose of nectar to attract bees to flowers, even though we personally do not experience it (first three suchnesses), appreciating that fact - no matter how small it is - is fundamental in developing a complete picture of the existence of flowers, ecosystems or indeed nature and reality itself. This culminates in:

  • Such a Whole (10): This is a complete view of the reality you are experiencing. It is true wondrous appreciation of experience. Someone who can truly appreciate such a whole finds as much wonder in this reality as the reality produced by LSD. Miracles are everywhere, nothing is inherently 'good' or 'bad', everything just is.

  • The purpose of Tathatā is to liberate an individual from 'good' or 'bad' and to simply appreciate the present as it is in it's utter reality. By realising that no two moments are identical and that the 'suchness' of each moment is unique and miraculous, each moment can be savoured without a care for 'good' or 'bad'. A person who truly practises tathatā can be lying on their death bed and be smiling at the miracle of experiencing death.

To practise Tathatā, at first you have to actively try to appreciate the three overarching stages - meditate on and appreciate what the experience is to you (first three) in terms of physical traits and emotions/thoughts evoked. Then meditate on and appreciate what the experience means in the larger picture (next six) in terms of purpose and the 'why' of it. Then simply enjoy it for what it is. The more you try to do this early on, the more you naturally will do this later on and you can discover a new degree of appreciation for the mundane.

An example of this applied to something negative is a breakup. At first, observe the breakup in it's discernible terms, you might observe that you shouted and got all hot and flustered and that they responded by sitting calmly and telling you 'it's over' or 'get out'. Doing this can help straighten the experience in your mind and gives you a solid base to work off. Now the emotional content: you are upset that it is over and angry at yourself for not 'seeing the signs'. Then after a while you might realise that it's better off this way, that if you couldn't solve the problems plaguing the relationship it might be better to just let go. Then you might become happy that - although it's over now - you had a good run (see how quickly the same experience can go from sad to neutral to happy? This is an example of the lack of 'good' or 'bad', events simply 'are') and you're happy that you had something so great that it could make you feel so sad. Now appreciate the function of the relationship - all of them: it used to drag you away from activities you enjoy, you had to give up a bit of volunteering or video games or gardening to work at it, you got to have sex pretty regularly, your parents were ever so happy/hated it/didn't care/weren't informed. And finally appreciate the relationship in it's entirety, without judgement, just as an experience you underwent. Then find wonder in the fact that such a miraculously complex thing could develop between two such miraculously complex organisms in the miraculously complex suchness that is existence. This is Tathatā.

Part II will concern itself with the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. I hope you enjoyed this and I'll crosslink all of this stuff with relevant comments/sources as they become available.
